catalog_quote: Primary stress within roots in Paku is on the penultimate syllable and is non-distinctive. Stress placement is very regular and predictable with only few exceptions in the data. What this means is that stress is not part of the lexical entry of a word. [...] Moreover there is both inter- and intra-speaker variation with regard to stress placement: not only do speakers sometimes vary from each other but also on occasion the same speaker will produce the same word differently without any obvious conditioning environment. An example of a root exhibiting a lot of variation is tekui ‘when’ which is sometimes produced as ['tekuj] and other times as [te'kuj]. A common example of irregular stress placement is bakoi ‘NEG’ in which the ultimate syllable is more prominent than the penultimate one. new_statements.quote: Primary stress within roots in Paku is on the penultimate syllable and is non-distinctive. Stress placement is very regular and predictable with only few exceptions in the data. What this means is that stress is not part of the lexical entry of a word. [...] Paku stress does not move to the right through suffixation. For instance, when -an is suffixed to the verbal root /'gawi/ 'work' to form /'gawian/ 'work (n.)', stress remains on the original penultimate syllable of /'gawi/. As a result, in /'gawian/ stress is now on the antepenultimate syllable. In the few instances of roots consisting of four syllables, in addition to primary stress on the penultimate syllable secondary stress is placed on the initial one, e.g. [,kolo'waNun] 'how' and [,wuwu'nijan] 'bladder'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root; it is non-contrastive and not lexical. Suffixation (-an) does not shift stress rightward, so suffixed words surface with antepenultimate stress. Stress is described as not a salient feature, with some free inter- and intra-speaker variation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In four-syllable roots, secondary stress on the initial syllable (e.g. [,kolo'waNun] 'how', [,wuwu'nijan] 'bladder').
new_statements.exceptions: Free variation in some roots (tekui 'when' ['tekuj]~[te'kuj]); bakoi 'NEG' regularly has final prominence; variability decreases with syllable count (none in four-syllable words); in content questions phrase stress falls on the question word (8.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root, not the word: stress stays on the root penult under suffixation (-> word-antepenult in -an forms); most Paku affixation is prefixal so root-penult = word-penult in most forms. Author notes intonation unit seems more relevant in discourse; stress judged impressionistically (no instrumental study).
new_statements.identity_note: Diedrich 2018 describes Paku (paku1239, ISO pku) as spoken in four villages (Tampa area) in southeast Central Kalimantan, ~50 speakers, moribund; East Barito (reclassified out of Southeast Barito per Smith 2017). No dialect split relevant to the stress statement.
